claim: Two rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) participated in the study with weights of 5-7 kg and ages of 5 and 7 years.
source: Two adult male Rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) participated in the study (weight: 5–7 kg, age: 5, 7 years).
evidence: Direct statement in the Materials and methods section describing the subjects.

claim: Experimental procedures were approved by the Ethics in Research Committee of the Institute of Neurobiology.
source: Experimental procedures were approved by the Ethics in Research Committee of the Institute of Neurobiology and were in agreement with the principles outlined in the Guide for Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (National Institutes of Health).
evidence: Direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: Each monkey was surgically implanted with titanium head bolts and a titanium recording chamber over the left supplementary motor area (SMA).
source: Each monkey was surgically implanted with titanium head bolts and a titanium recording chamber over the left supplementary motor area (SMA).
evidence: Direct statement about surgical procedures.

claim: Placement of the recording chambers over the SMA was guided by structural MRI for both monkeys.
source: Placement of the chambers over the SMA was guided by structural MRI for both monkeys (Figure 1E).
evidence: Statement about chamber placement methodology with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: The recording chamber on monkey 1 was centered 23 mm anterior to Ear Bar Zero and 4 mm lateral to the midline, on the left hemisphere.
source: The recoding chamber on monkey 1 (shown) was centered 23 mm anterior to Ear Bar Zero and 4 mm lateral to the midline, on the left hemisphere.
evidence: Specific coordinates provided in Figure 1E caption.

claim: Monkeys performed a visual metronome task while maintaining eye and hand fixation over a touch screen.
source: Monkeys were trained in a visual metronome task described in detail in a previous report (García-Garibay et al., 2016). Briefly, while maintain eye and hand fixation over a touch screen (ELO Touch Solutions, model 1939L; ASL Eye-Track 6), subjects observed a visual stimulus (gray circle, 10° diameter, 25° eccentricity) that periodically changed position from one side of the screen to the other, at regular intervals (entrainment epoch; 500, 750, or 1000 ms interval; pseudo-randomly selected on each trial; Figure 1A).
evidence: Description of the behavioral task with citation to previous work.

claim: The visual stimulus was a gray circle with 10° diameter and 25° eccentricity.
source: subjects observed a visual stimulus (gray circle, 10° diameter, 25° eccentricity) that periodically changed position from one side of the screen to the other
evidence: Specific parameters of the visual stimulus.

claim: Interval durations were pseudo-randomly chosen to be 500, 750, or 1000 ms on each trial.
source: On each trial, the interval duration was pseudo-randomly chosen to be 500, 750, or 1000 ms.
evidence: Direct statement about interval selection.

claim: Monkeys correctly estimated the stimulus location in more than 80% of trials.
source: The behavioral results show that monkeys satisfactorily performed the task and were able to correctly estimate the location of the stimulus in more than 80% of trials (94 ± 0.2% monkey 1; 86 ± 0.3% monkey 2; mean ± s.e. over sessions, n = 131 sessions).
evidence: Quantitative behavioral performance data across sessions.

claim: Monkey 1 achieved 94 ± 0.2% correct responses.
source: 94 ± 0.2% monkey 1
evidence: Specific performance metric for monkey 1.

claim: Monkey 2 achieved 86 ± 0.3% correct responses.
source: 86 ± 0.3% monkey 2
evidence: Specific performance metric for monkey 2.

claim: Performance was significantly above chance level (p<0.001).
source: Performance was significantly above chance (broken line at p=0.5; z-test p<0.001; n = 131 sessions; median ±I.Q.R. over sessions).
evidence: Statistical test result reported in Figure 1B caption.

claim: The proportion of correct responses declined as a function of the number of maintenance intervals.
source: Importantly, performance as a function of time displays the hallmark of a timing task: the proportion of correct responses declines as a function of the number of maintenance intervals (or equivalently, elapsed time).
evidence: Description of behavioral pattern observed in the data.

claim: The proportion of correct responses started close to 100% and declined to approximately 75% for the last maintenance intervals.
source: The proportion of correct responses started close to 100% and declined to approximately 75% for the last maintenance intervals (last two data points for each curve).
evidence: Quantitative description of performance decline.

claim: The decline in performance is consistent with the internal rhythm gradually drifting away from the true tempo of the stimulus.
source: This behavior is consistent with the internal rhythm gradually drifting away from the true tempo of the stimulus (Gibbon et al., 1997; Grondin, 2001).
evidence: Interpretation of behavioral pattern with supporting citations.

claim: The performance pattern is well captured by a model in which the subject's time estimates arise from increasingly noisy distributions described by Weber's Law of time.
source: As we described in previous work (García-Garibay et al., 2016), this pattern is well captured by a model in which the subject's time estimates arise from increasingly noisy (wider) distributions, described by Weber's Law of time (also called the scalar property of timing) (Laje et al., 2011).
evidence: Model fitting to behavioral data with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Reaction times to the go-cue increase significantly in proportion to elapsed time.
source: Reaction times to the go-cue increases significantly in proportion to elapsed time within a narrow window ranging between 350 ms after the first maintenance interval of the fastest tempo (500 ms intervals), to 400 ms after the last interval of the slowest tempo (1000 ms intervals) (Figure 1C; R2 = 0.72, slope = 11 ms/s, p<0.001; monkey 1 = 10.2 ms/s±0.8; monkey 2 = 11.3 ms/s ± 0.5).
evidence: Statistical analysis of reaction time data with regression results.

claim: The linear regression of reaction times has R² = 0.72, slope = 11 ms/s, p<0.001.
evidence: Statistical parameters from regression analysis.

claim: Monkey 1 showed a reaction time slope of 10.2 ms/s ± 0.8.
source: monkey 1 = 10.2 ms/s±0.8
evidence: Individual subject data for reaction time slope.

claim: Monkey 2 showed a reaction time slope of 11.3 ms/s ± 0.5.
source: monkey 2 = 11.3 ms/s ± 0.5
evidence: Individual subject data for reaction time slope.

claim: Neural activity was recorded in 131 experimental sessions (84 for monkey 1 and 47 for monkey 2).
source: While the monkeys performed the visual metronome task, we recorded neural activity in 131 experimental sessions (84 and 47 for monkeys 1 and 2, respectively; Figure 1E)
evidence: Direct statement about number of recording sessions.

claim: Local field potentials (LFPs) were analyzed within the 5–80 Hz band.
source: we recorded neural activity in 131 experimental sessions (84 and 47 for monkeys 1 and 2, respectively; Figure 1E), and analyzed the local field potentials (LFPs) within 5–80 Hz band.
evidence: Description of LFP analysis parameters.

claim: LFP power in the gamma band (30-40 Hz) was up to two-fold larger than baseline activity (p<0.001).
source: In this band, LFP power was up to two-fold larger than the baseline activity recorded 500 ms before trial initiation (p<0.001; permutation test of the time-frequency bins, 1000 permutations).
evidence: Statistical comparison of gamma power to baseline with permutation test.

claim: The average gamma amplitude at the time of switches was significantly higher than halfway between them (t-test, p<0.01 for the three tempos).
source: To test this observation quantitatively, we verified that the average gamma amplitude at the time of switches was significantly higher than halfway between them (t-test, p<0.01 for the three tempos; window sizes 1/4th of interval length; see Materials and methods).
evidence: Statistical test comparing gamma amplitude at different time points.

claim: Gamma oscillations are composed of transient bursts during which oscillations increase in amplitude.
source: The LFP recordings from single trials (band-passed at 30–40 Hz) revealed short-duration bursts during which the oscillations transiently increase in amplitude (Figure 2B), consistent with recent findings in the putamen (Bartolo et al., 2014) and the prefrontal cortex (Lundqvist et al., 2016).
evidence: Description of gamma burst characteristics with citations to similar findings.

claim: Gamma bursts during maintenance tend to coincide with the times at which the stimulus would have changed position.
source: Importantly, we observed that during the maintenance epoch, these bursts tended to coincide with the times at which the stimulus would have changed position, as is shown by the peaks in the spectrogram of the example single trials (Figure 2A).
evidence: Observation from single trial analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Gamma bursts were defined as periods in which gamma amplitude exceeded the 90th percentile of the amplitude distribution across trials for at least 100 ms.
source: Bursts were defined as the period in which gamma amplitude exceeded the 90th percentile of the amplitude distribution across trials, for at least 100 ms (four cycles of the gamma rhythm).
evidence: Methodological definition of gamma bursts.

claim: Gamma bursts have a stereotyped temporal shape and increase in amplitude after each consecutive transition.
source: The bursts have a stereotyped temporal shape and increase in amplitude after each consecutive transition.
evidence: Description of gamma burst characteristics across transitions.

claim: The amplitude of gamma bursts increased in proportion to the time elapsed since the initiation of the internal rhythm (R² = 0.86, exponential model).
source: Importantly, we found that the amplitude of these bursts increased in proportion to the time elapsed since the initiation of the internal rhythm (Figure 3C; R2 = 0.86, exponential model).
evidence: Statistical model fitting to gamma burst amplitude data.

claim: On fast tempo trials (500 ms interval), the dynamics of gamma on error trials was right-shifted with respect to correct trials.
source: The results showed that, on fast tempo trials (500 ms interval), the dynamics of gamma on error trials was right-shifted with respect to correct trials. That is, error trials displayed slower dynamics compared to correct trials (Figure 4A, upper panel).
evidence: Comparison of gamma dynamics between correct and error trials.

claim: Error trials on fast tempo (500 ms) oscillated at lower frequencies compared to correct trials.
source: This trend was captured by the power spectrums of error and correct trials, which showed that error trials indeed oscillated at lower frequencies (Figure 4A, inset on upper panel).
evidence: Power spectrum analysis of error vs correct trials.

claim: On slow tempo trials (1000 ms), the dynamics of errors resemble a left-shifted version of the correct trials.
source: Conversely, the dynamics of errors on slow tempo trials (1000 ms) resemble a left-shifted version of the correct trials, that is errors displayed faster dynamics as compared to the correct trials (Figure 4A; bottom panel).
evidence: Comparison of gamma dynamics for slow tempo trials.

claim: Error trials on slow tempo (1000 ms) oscillated at higher frequencies compared to correct trials.
source: This pattern is captured by the power spectrums of correct and error trials, which show that error trials oscillated at higher frequencies compared to correct trials (Figure 4A, inset on the bottom panel).
evidence: Power spectrum analysis showing frequency differences.

claim: Correct and error trials can be classified with increasing accuracy as a function of elapsed time.
source: This analysis shows that correct and error trials are increasingly easier to classify as a function of elapsed time, just as it would be expected from a rhythm that increasingly falls out of sync with the correct tempo.
evidence: Results from logistic classifier analysis.

claim: Neural recordings were performed with seven independent movable microelectrodes (2–3 MΩ).
source: Neural recordings were performed with seven independent movable microelectrodes (2–3 MΩ, Thomas Recordings, Giessen, Germany).
evidence: Description of recording equipment.

claim: Spikes were sampled at 30 KHz.
source: At each recording site, spikes were isolated online (Cerebus acquisition system, Blackrock Microsystems, Salt Lake City, UT) and sampled at 30 KHz.
evidence: Technical specification of spike recording.

claim: Local field potentials (LFPs) were obtained by filtering the electrode signal at 0.5 to 500 Hz, at a 2 KHz rate.
source: The local field potentials (LFPs) were obtained by filtering the electrode signal at 0.5 to 500 Hz, at a 2 KHz rate.
evidence: Technical specification of LFP recording.

claim: Offline, the LFP signal was down sampled to 1 KHz and band-pass filtered to the 2–50 Hz band.
source: Offline, the signal was down sampled to 1 KHz, and band-pass filtered to the 2–50 Hz band.
evidence: Description of offline signal processing.

claim: A 200 ms window sliding at 5 ms steps was used for the time-frequency maps.
source: A 200 ms windows sliding at 5 ms steps was used for the time-frequency maps (one taper was used, 5 Hz bandwidth).
evidence: Methodological parameters for spectral analysis.

claim: Spectrogram power was normalized by dividing each frequency and time bin by the average power in a 500 ms baseline window before trial initiation.
source: Spectrogram power was normalized by dividing each frequency and time bin by the average power in a 500 ms baseline window before trial initiation.
evidence: Description of normalization procedure.

claim: 113 neurons were recorded (78 from monkey 1 and 35 from monkey 2).
source: Simultaneously with LFPs, we recorded the extracellular spike potentials of 113 neurons (78 monkey 1; 35 monkey 2).
evidence: Direct statement about number of recorded neurons.

claim: The temporal profile of the mean firing rates largely resembled the modulations of gamma-band activity in the LFP.
source: The temporal profile of the mean firing rates largely resembled the modulations of gamma-band activity in the LFP in the sense that firing rates (1) display oscillatory amplitude modulations, both during entrainment and maintenance intervals (Figure 7A,B); (2) firing rates increase as a function of total elapsed time; and (3) the activity of neurons in the delayed-reach task increase during the period preceding reach movements to a target signaled by a brief visual cue (Figure 7C).
evidence: Comparison of firing rate patterns to LFP gamma activity.

claim: Of the 113 recorded neurons, 74 preferred the right side of the screen and 39 preferred the left side.
source: Of the 113 recorded neurons, 74 preferred the right side of the screen, and 39 preferred the left side (Materials and methods).
evidence: Quantification of spatial preference in recorded neurons.

claim: The LFP activity simultaneously recorded with each spike has a power peak at 30 Hz.
source: We found that the LFP activity simultaneously recorded with each spike has a power peak at 30 Hz, and this peak is especially salient during maintenance intervals (Figure 8A, bottom panel; factorial ANOVA: interaction band/condition F = 12.11 p<0.05, Bonferroni tests of Gamma power in maintenance and entrainment vs baseline: p<0.05).
evidence: Spike-triggered average analysis with statistical testing.

claim: The association between spikes and the 25–40 Hz frequency band is stronger at the times of stimulus transitions (t-test p<0.005).
source: Moreover, the association between spikes and the 25–40 Hz frequency band is stronger at the times of stimulus transitions, that is. around the times at which the stimulus switches from one side of the screen to the other (Figure 8C; window length around switch: half an interval, t-test p<0.005).
evidence: Statistical test of spike-LFP association at different time points.

claim: Jittering spike times by ±15 ms resulted in loss of the observed peak at the gamma band (t test p=0.21).
source: To demonstrate that gamma is closely associated with the timing of spikes we performed a control analysis in which we jittered the spike times by ±15 ms with the resulting loss of the observed peak at the gamma band (random uniform distribution; grey traces Figure 8c; t test between jittered data in switch and non-switch conditions p=0.21).
evidence: Control analysis demonstrating temporal specificity of spike-gamma association.

claim: Coherence between LFPs in simultaneously recorded electrodes decayed as a function of electrode distance (R² = 0.72).
source: The results show that coherence decayed as a function of electrode distance (Figure 8D, R2 = 0.72), as expected by an LFP signal that is generated in the neuronal circuits within the vicinity of the recording electrode.
evidence: Analysis of LFP coherence as function of distance.

claim: Monkeys can maintain rhythms in the absence of sensory stimuli and in the absence of overt motor commands.
source: Our results show that (1) monkeys can maintain rhythms in the absence of sensory stimuli and in the absence of overt motor commands.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding.

claim: Internal rhythms are encoded by bursts of low gamma-band LFP oscillations in SMA whose timing and amplitude indicate rhythm intervals and total elapsed time, respectively.
source: (2) Those internal rhythms are encoded by bursts of low gamma-band LFP oscillations in SMA whose timing and amplitude indicate rhythm intervals and total elapsed time, respectively.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding about neural encoding.

claim: The spikes of single neurons are associated with the low gamma band frequency of the LFP.
source: (3) The spikes of single neurons are associated with the low gamma band frequency of the LFP, which is consistent with the idea that gamma oscillations might help to synchronize populations of neurons whose temporally coincident firing would have a larger impact on its postsynaptic targets (Buzsáki and Schomburg, 2015; Cardin et al., 2009; Fries, 2015; Siegle et al., 2014; Veit et al., 2017; Womelsdorf et al., 2007; Wong et al., 2016).
evidence: Summary statement with interpretation and citations to supporting literature.

claim: SMA plays a central role in learning, imaging, planning and executing complex motor actions.
source: SMA plays a central role in learning, imaging, planning and executing complex motor actions (Nachev et al., 2008; Romo and Schultz, 1992; Kurata and Wise, 1988; Shima and Tanji, 2000; Murakami et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about SMA function with multiple supporting citations.

claim: SMA is densely and reciprocally connected to M1 and to the parietal and frontal lobes, and has direct projections to motor nuclei in the brain stem.
source: It is densely and reciprocally connected to M1 and to the parietal and frontal lobes, and has direct projections to motor nuclei in the brain stem (Jürgens, 1984).
evidence: Statement about SMA connectivity with citation.

claim: SMA activity has been found to correlate not only with motor actions but also with cognitive, emotional, and perceptual functions.
source: Thanks to this diverse input and output relationships its activity been found to correlate not only with motor actions but also with cognitive, emotional, and perceptual functions (Narayana et al., 2012; Vergara et al., 2016; de Lafuente and Romo, 2005).
evidence: Statement about SMA functional correlates with citations.

claim: SMA is active before the actual movement begins, participating in action selection and determining the time at which actions are performed.
source: SMA is active before the actual movement begins, participating in action selection, and importantly, determining the time at which actions are performed (Merchant and Averbeck, 2017; Mita et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2010; Ohara et al., 2001; Yokoyama et al., 2016; Shima and Tanji, 2000).
evidence: Statement about SMA timing function with multiple citations.

claim: Preparatory activity can be observed even when monkeys are required to rapidly produce a movement in response to a sensory cue.
source: Preparatory activity can be observed even when monkeys are required to rapidly produce a movement in response to a sensory cue (Lara et al., 2018)
evidence: Statement about preparatory activity with citation.

claim: Preparatory activity constitutes the initial step of the temporal evolution of a dynamical system for the control of movement.
source: it has been proposed that this preparatory activity constitutes the initial step of the temporal evolution of a dynamical system for the control of movement (Churchland et al., 2010; Remington et al., 2018).
evidence: Theoretical interpretation with citations.

claim: LFP and single neuron activity in SMA starts during the entrainment epoch of the metronome task, seconds before an actual movement will be required.
source: Consistent with this view, our results show that LFP and single neuron activity in SMA starts during the entrainment epoch of the metronome task, seconds before an actual movement will be required.
evidence: Observation from the current study's data.

claim: The internal metronome is encoded as a dynamic motor plan that is initiated by the presentation of entrainment intervals.
source: Thus, the internal metronome is encoded as a dynamic motor plan that is initiated by the presentation of entrainment intervals.
evidence: Interpretive conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: The tempo of the internal metronome is encoded by the timing, not the amplitude of the gamma bursts.
source: However, we must note that the tempo of the internal metronome is encoded by the timing, not the amplitude of the gamma bursts.
evidence: Clarification of the encoding mechanism.

claim: Error trials are not explained by random behavioral responses but are due to the internal metronome lagging or getting ahead of the true tempo.
source: Even on error trials, gamma activity, and the firing pattern of neurons, show rhythmic dynamics and a mean amplitude that increases with total elapsed time. Thus, there are three independent lines of evidence supporting the notion that error trials arise from the internal metronome falling out of sync with the intended tempo.
evidence: Interpretation of error trial patterns.

claim: Gamma synchronization might be useful to the formation of local ensembles of neurons that increase the temporal coordination of presynaptic spikes on postsynaptic targets.
source: Gamma synchronization might be useful to the formation of local ensembles of neurons that increase the temporal coordination of presynaptic spikes on postsynaptic targets, allowing brief windows of effective communication (Wong et al., 2016; Womelsdorf et al., 2007; Buzsáki and Schomburg, 2015).
evidence: Theoretical interpretation with citations.

claim: Previous results show that gamma oscillations increase before the execution of a motor action, and then shut down at the time of movement onset.
source: Previous results show that gamma oscillations increase before the execution of a motor action, and then shut down at the time of movement onset (Yokoyama et al., 2016) a result replicated by our data.
evidence: Citation to previous work and confirmation in current study.

claim: Previous work by Merchant and colleagues found that LFP gamma band activity in the basal ganglia was associated with the presentation of sensory stimuli defining the intervals within a hand tapping task.
source: Previous work by Merchant and colleagues found that LFP gamma band activity in the basal ganglia was associated with the presentation of sensory stimuli defining the intervals within a hand tapping task (Bartolo et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to related previous work.

claim: Merchant and colleagues found that bursts of gamma were selective for intervals of different durations, and thus different cell populations were selective for different time intervals.
source: They found that bursts of gamma were selective for intervals of different durations, and thus different cell populations were selective for different time intervals.
evidence: Description of findings from cited work.

claim: In SMA cortex, no duration selectivity was found; instead, gamma bursts encoded intervals of different durations.
source: We found no such duration selectivity in the SMA cortex, instead observing that gamma bursts encoded intervals of different durations.
evidence: Contrast between current findings and previous work.

claim: Signals associated with timing tasks can be found across multiple brain areas, including parietal, motor, and premotor cortices, as well as dopaminergic midbrain neuron in the primate.
source: Signals associated with timing tasks can be found across multiple brain areas, including parietal, motor, and premotor cortices, as well as dopaminergic midbrain neuron in the primate (Ghose and Maunsell, 2002; Genovesio et al., 2006; Lebedev and Wise, 2000; Mita et al., 2009; Harrington et al., 2010).
evidence: Summary of literature on timing signals with citations.

claim: Jazayeri and Shadlen showed that activity of single neurons in the lateral intraparietal area encodes the time elapsed from a previous sensory stimuli, as well as the time remaining to initiate a saccadic eye movement.
source: For example, Jazayeri and Shadlen, 2015 have shown that activity of single neurons in the lateral intraparietal area encodes the time elapsed from a previous sensory stimuli, as well as the time remaining to initiate a saccadic eye movement (Jazayeri and Shadlen, 2015).
evidence: Citation to specific previous finding.

claim: Jazayeri and colleagues demonstrated that encoding intervals of different lengths is achieved by means of speeding up or slowing down the temporal dynamics of populations of neurons.
source: A recent important result by Jazayeri and colleagues demonstrated that encoding intervals of different lengths is achieved by means of speeding up or slowing down the temporal dynamics of populations of neurons that, individually, display widely different firing patterns (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Citation to recent related work.

claim: The current results extend the finding of temporal scaling to the dynamics of the LFP oscillations.
source: Our results extend this finding to the dynamics of the LFP oscillations by demonstrating that they also show temporal scaling (Figures 3A and 6C).
evidence: Statement connecting current findings to previous work.

claim: Time-estimation and time-production signals are present as dynamic motor plans that are distributed across the motor structures that participate in executing timely motor actions.
source: A coherent picture is thus emerging, indicating that time-estimation and time-production signals are present as dynamic motor plans that are distributed across the motor structures that participate in executing timely motor actions.
evidence: Synthetic conclusion integrating current and previous findings.

claim: Gamma amplitude increased throughout the trial, providing an estimate of total elapsed time.
source: Moreover, gamma amplitude increased throughout the trial, providing an estimate of total elapsed time.
evidence: Summary statement from abstract about gamma amplitude encoding.

claim: The timing of gamma bursts and firing rate modulations allowed predicting whether monkeys were ahead or behind the correct tempo.
source: Notably, the timing of gamma bursts and firing rate modulations allowed predicting whether monkeys were ahead or behind the correct tempo.
evidence: Summary statement from abstract about predictive value of neural signals.

claim: SMA uses dynamic motor plans to encode a metronome for rhythms and a stopwatch for total elapsed time.
source: Our results indicate that SMA uses dynamic motor plans to encode a metronome for rhythms and a stopwatch for total elapsed time.
evidence: Main conclusion statement from abstract.

claim: Nonhuman primates and other vertebrates are capable of synchronizing their movements to periodic rhythms.
source: Nonhuman primates and other vertebrates are capable synchronizing their movements to periodic rhythms (Merchant et al., 2013; Takeya et al., 2017; Gámez et al., 2018)
evidence: Statement about animal capabilities with citations.

claim: Monkeys can internally maintain rhythms of different tempos in the absence of overt motor actions.
source: we recently showed that monkeys can internally maintain rhythms of different tempos in the absence of overt motor actions (García-Garibay et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Cortical and subcortical motor circuits participate in behavioral tasks that require time perception and temporally precise behavioral responses.
source: Ample evidence indicates that cortical and subcortical motor circuits participate in behavioral tasks that require time perception and temporally precise behavioral responses (Mita et al., 2009; Crowe et al., 2014; Bartolo et al., 2014; Merchant and Averbeck, 2017; Grahn and Brett, 2007; Ivry and Spencer, 2004; Murray et al., 2014).
evidence: Summary of literature with multiple citations.

claim: The neuronal mechanisms that allow motor structures to encode rhythms of different tempos, in the absence of motor commands, are not yet completely understood.
source: Nonetheless, the neuronal mechanisms that allow motor structures to encode rhythms of different tempos, in the absence of motor commands, are not yet completely understood.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap motivating the study.

claim: The intervals defining the rhythm are encoded by the periodic onset of gamma bursts.
source: Our results show that bursts of lower gamma band activity (30–40 Hz) reflect the internally maintained tempos by a simple mechanism: the intervals defining the rhythm are encoded by the periodic onset of gamma bursts.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding about encoding mechanism.

claim: Gamma bursts encoded both rhythm and the total elapsed time in the absence of sensory stimulation and overt motor activity.
source: Importantly, gamma bursts encoded both rhythm and the total elapsed time in the absence of sensory stimulation and overt motor activity.
evidence: Summary statement emphasizing key finding.

claim: Gamma responses to stimulus onset are similar only during the first 500 ms of the first entrainment interval, which is the only epoch in which monkeys have no information about the metronome tempo.
source: In fact, gamma responses to stimulus onset are similar only during the first 500 ms of the first entrainment interval, which is the only epoch in which monkeys have no information about the metronome tempo (Figure 6C).
evidence: Observation about gamma responses during initial learning phase.

claim: Gamma bursts reflect cognitive processes related to estimating the rhythm of the visual metronome.
source: These results indicate that gamma bursts reflect cognitive processes related to estimating the rhythm of the visual metronome.
evidence: Interpretive conclusion about the nature of gamma bursts.

claim: Burst amplitude increased linearly in proportion to total elapsed time during entrainment intervals (R² = 0.94).
source: We found that burst amplitude increased linearly in proportion to total elapsed time (R2 = 0.94).
evidence: Statistical model fitting to burst amplitude data during entrainment.

claim: The SMA circuit reflected the total elapsed time since the beginning of the entrainment epoch through gamma burst amplitude.
source: In this manner, in addition to periodically generating bursts in each entrainment interval, the SMA circuit reflected the total elapsed time since the beginning of the entrainment epoch.
evidence: Summary of dual encoding mechanism.

claim: The cross-correlogram for the 500 and 750 ms intervals peak at negative lags, demonstrating that incorrect trials lag behind the correct tempo.
source: The cross-correlogram for the 500 and 750 ms intervals peak at negative lags, demonstrating that incorrect trials lag behind the correct tempo.
evidence: Result from cross-correlation analysis of firing rates.

claim: For the slow tempo (1000 ms), the opposite pattern was observed, with errors getting ahead of the correct tempo.
source: The opposite pattern was observed for the slow tempo (1000 ms tempo).
evidence: Result from cross-correlation analysis for slow tempo.

claim: The power of the spike-triggered average around 30 Hz was significantly larger during entrainment and maintenance compared to baseline (p<0.01).
source: This analysis demonstrated that the average power of the STA over the gamma band was significantly larger during entrainment and maintenance, as compared to the baseline period (p<0.01; Figure 8B).
evidence: Statistical result from spike-triggered average analysis.

claim: The LFP signals recorded reflect local interaction and were not the result of signals being volume-conducted from other brain regions.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that the LFP signals we recorded reflect local interaction and were not the result of signals being volume-conducted from other brain regions.
evidence: Conclusion from coherence analysis.

claim: In the delayed-reach task, monkeys were required to wait a variable delay period before making a reach movement to one side of the screen signaled by a brief visual stimulus.
source: In this task, monkeys were required wait a variable delay period before making a reach movement to one side of the screen signaled by a brief visual stimulus (Figure 5).
evidence: Description of control task design.

claim: The stimulus in the delayed-reach task appeared for 500 ms on either the left or right side of the screen.
source: The stimulus appeared for 500 ms on either the left or side of the screen (randomly selected)
evidence: Specific parameter of control task.

claim: The delay period in the delayed-reach task was randomly selected from a truncated exponential distribution with a minimum delay duration of 1.1 s and a maximum of 3 s.
source: the delay period was randomly selected from a truncated exponential distribution with a minimum delay duration of 1.1 s and a maximum of 3 s.
evidence: Specific parameter of control task delay period.

claim: As monkeys prepare an impending reach movement in the delayed-reach task, the LFPs in SMA generate bursts of gamma band activity that occur more frequently, and with increasing amplitude, as a function of total elapsed time.
source: The results of this control task show that, as monkeys prepare an impending reach movement, the LFPs in SMA generate bursts of gamma band activity that occur more frequently, and with increasing amplitude, as a function of total elapsed time (Figure 5C, delay period).
evidence: Result from delayed-reach control task.

claim: The results of the delayed-reach control task are consistent with the idea that gamma bursts in SMA encode impending motor commands.
source: These findings are consistent with the idea that gamma bursts in SMA encode impending motor commands.
evidence: Interpretation of control task results.

claim: The results of the delayed-reach control task are consistent with the idea that the SMA circuits reflect internal rhythms by means of rhythmically alternating motor plans to make a reach movement to the left and right locations of the screen.
source: Moreover, the results of this control task are consistent with the idea that the SMA circuits reflect internal rhythms by means of rhythmically alternating motor plans to make a reach movement to the left and right locations of the screen.
evidence: Interpretation connecting control task to main task.

claim: Gamma bursts are not merely sensory responses to visual stimuli during entrainment intervals.
source: A potential concern is that the gamma bursts in entrainment intervals are merely sensory responses to visual stimuli. However, a pure sensory response should produce similar gamma dynamics after each stimulus presentation, both across consecutive entrainment intervals (1st, 2nd, 3rd), and also similar across tempos (500, 750, 1000 ms), which was clearly not the case in our results (Figure 6A).
evidence: Argument against alternative interpretation with data reference.

claim: Gamma bursts carry information about the animals' knowledge that the third entrainment interval was the last visible interval.
source: Therefore, gamma bursts carry information about the animals' knowledge that the third entrainment interval was the last visible interval, that is the last interval that could be used for estimating the tempo.
evidence: Inference about cognitive information encoded in gamma bursts.

claim: Gamma dynamics likely incorporate aspects of higher cognitive processing.
source: Thus, gamma dynamics likely incorporate aspects of higher cognitive processing.
evidence: Interpretive conclusion about the nature of gamma activity.

claim: The temporal profiles of gamma onset times significantly differ both across consecutive intervals and across metronome tempos (p<0.01).
source: The tests demonstrated that the temporal profiles of gamma onset times significantly differ, both across consecutive intervals and across metronome tempos (p<0.01; corrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: Statistical test result comparing gamma onset distributions.

claim: Rhythms of different tempos are supported by the presence of rhythmic neuronal activity outlining each individual interval.
source: Our results now reveal that rhythms of different tempos are supported by the presence of rhythmic neuronal activity outlining each individual interval.
evidence: Summary statement about neural mechanism for rhythm encoding.

claim: In addition to rhythmic activity, the increases in gamma burst amplitude and mean firing rates provide information about total elapsed time.
source: In addition to this, the increases in gamma burst amplitude, and mean firing rates, provide information about total elapsed time.
evidence: Summary of dual encoding mechanism.

claim: Larger gamma band amplitudes are correlated with increased reaction times.
source: We also demonstrate that larger gamma band amplitudes are correlated with increased reaction times.
evidence: Result from correlation analysis mentioned in context of Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gamma band activity decreases before movement initiation, and lower frequencies appear after movement initiation.
source: Note how gamma activity decreases before movement initiation, and lower frequencies appear after movement initiation.
evidence: Observation from LFP spectrogram aligned to movement onset.

claim: The decrease in performance as a function of elapsed time is expected from variability of the subjects' internal timing in the absence of the external visual rhythm.
source: The decrease in performance as a function of elapsed time is expected from variability of the subjects' internal timing in the absence of the external visual rhythm.
evidence: Explanation of behavioral pattern in Figure 1B caption.

claim: The drop in performance was captured by a model of timing subject to scalar variability.
source: This drop in performance was captured by a model of timing subject to scalar variability (continuous lines).
evidence: Description of model fit shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Signal amplitude in the spectrogram was normalized with respect to a 500 ms baseline period before stimulus presentation.
source: Signal amplitude was normalized with respect to a 500 ms baseline period before stimulus presentation.
evidence: Methodological detail from Figure 1D caption.

claim: A salient modulation of the LFP signal is observed around the gamma band (30–40 Hz).
source: A salient modulation of the LFP signal is observed around the gamma band (30–40 Hz).
evidence: Observation from spectrogram in Figure 1D.

claim: Gamma activity rhythmically increases in sync with the left-right transitions of the stimulus.
source: Gamma activity rhythmically increases in sync with the left-right transitions of the stimulus.
evidence: Observation from Figure 1D spectrogram.

claim: There is an increase in gamma activity as a function of total elapsed time.
source: Note also the increase in gamma activity as a function of total elapsed time.
evidence: Observation from Figure 1D spectrogram.
